step: Apply for Non-Immigrant B (business) visa at the Royal Thai Embassy or Consulate in the employee's home country; this entry permission is mandatory before travelling to Thailand for work
authority: Royal Thai Embassy / Consulate (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Thailand)
deadline_label: Minimum 15 business days before planned arrival date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign nationals who intend to work in Thailand must obtain a Non-Immigrant B category visa from a Royal Thai Embassy or Consulate before entering Thailand.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Entering Thailand on a visa exemption stamp or tourist visa and attempting to begin work or convert status in-country is not routinely possible and constitutes working without authorisation, which is a criminal offence. The Non-Immigrant B must be secured before boarding the outbound flight — attempting to apply for it on arrival or after entry will not succeed.
non_obvious_action_required: As soon as the employment offer is confirmed, book an appointment at the nearest Royal Thai Embassy. Required documents typically include an employer invitation letter on Thai company letterhead, a certified copy of the company DBD certificate of incorporation, the employee's academic credentials, two passport photographs, and the completed application form. Processing times vary from 3 to 15 business days depending on the embassy; allow extra time for smaller posts.
source: Immigration Bureau of Thailand — Non-Immigrant Visa Category B

step: Employer prepares and submits Form WP.3 (work permit employer petition) to the Department of Employment; the petition must be filed and approved before the employee performs any work in Thailand
authority: Department of Employment, Ministry of Labour
deadline_label: File before or on the day of employee arrival
non_obvious_official_guidance: An employer wishing to employ a foreign national in Thailand must submit a petition (Form WP.3) to the Department of Employment before the employee commences any work.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The WP.3 employer petition and the WP.10 employee work permit book are two distinct sequential steps processed at the same Department of Employment office but on separate occasions. The employer must file WP.3 first; the employee can only receive the physical WP.10 after the DOE approves the petition. The employee must not perform any work — including emails or calls on behalf of the Thai entity — while either step is pending. Additionally, employers must generally maintain a minimum ratio of four Thai employees to every one foreign employee, subject to exceptions by business type and treaty.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a Thai immigration or labour law firm at least four weeks before the employee's planned arrival. The WP.3 dossier requires: company DBD registration certificate, company VAT registration, shareholder list, most recent audited financial statements, evidence of the 4:1 Thai-to-foreign employee headcount ratio, and a detailed position description justifying the need for a foreign hire. Submit to the DOE office covering the employee's designated work location.
source: Department of Employment — Foreign Worker Permit Application (WP.3)

step: Employee obtains a police clearance certificate from their home country, apostilled and with a certified Thai-language translation, for inclusion in the work permit application dossier
authority: Home-country police authority; accepted by Department of Employment Thailand
deadline_label: Allow at least 6 weeks before planned arrival — apostille and translation add significant lead time
non_obvious_official_guidance: A police clearance certificate from the employee's country of nationality or most recent long-term country of residence is required as part of the work permit application documents submitted to the Department of Employment.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The certificate must be apostilled in the issuing country under the Hague Apostille Convention and then accompanied by a certified Thai-language translation from a recognised translation service. In several countries — including US FBI background checks and UK ACRO/DBS certificates — processing the clearance alone takes 4–10 weeks before apostille. Missing or improperly certified police clearance certificates are the most common single cause of work permit application delays or rejections in Thailand.
non_obvious_action_required: Initiate the police clearance request on the day relocation is confirmed. Identify whether the issuing country is a signatory to the Hague Apostille Convention and obtain the apostille from the designated competent authority (not just a notary). Source a certified Thai translation from a court-recognised translation service. Submit the original document — most DOE offices do not accept copies.
source: Department of Employment — Work Permit Required Documents

step: Employee obtains a medical certificate from a licensed physician confirming the absence of the five prohibited diseases specified in Ministerial Regulation (leprosy, tuberculosis, drug addiction, elephantiasis, third-stage syphilis)
authority: Department of Employment, Ministry of Labour
deadline_label: Within 30 days before work permit application — must be recent
source: Department of Employment — Work Permit Required Documents

step: Employer engages a Thai tax adviser to conduct a permanent establishment (PE) risk assessment before deploying the employee — determines whether the employee's activities in Thailand may expose the foreign company to Thai corporate income tax
deadline_label: Before deployment is confirmed — do not wait until the employee has arrived
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the Revenue Code of Thailand and applicable double-tax treaties, a foreign company may create a permanent establishment in Thailand if an employee habitually concludes contracts on behalf of the foreign company, maintains a fixed place of business in Thailand, or provides services there for a sufficient period defined under the treaty.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many employers assume that structuring the Thai payroll through a local entity, or holding a work permit for the employee, insulates the foreign parent from Thai corporate income tax exposure. It does not. The PE determination is made under the applicable double-tax treaty based on the nature and authority of the employee's activities — not on payroll structure. A PE finding exposes the foreign company to Thai corporate income tax at 20% on attributable profits and triggers ongoing filing obligations for the foreign entity with the Revenue Department.
non_obvious_action_required: Before confirming deployment, provide a Thai tax adviser with: (1) the double-tax treaty between Thailand and the employer's home jurisdiction; (2) a detailed description of the employee's planned activities and decision-making authority; (3) the proposed employment contract and any secondment agreement. Draft the scope-of-authority clause in the contract to minimise PE triggers under the treaty PE article, and document the economic rationale for the Thai presence.
source: Revenue Department of Thailand — Corporate Income Tax and Double Tax Treaties

step: House-master, building owner, or occupant files Form TM.30 with the Immigration Bureau to notify of the foreign national's stay at their premises — must be filed within 24 hours of the employee's arrival at that address
deadline_label: Within 24 hours of arrival at the accommodation address
non_obvious_official_guidance: Section 38 of the Immigration Act B.E. 2522 requires the house-master, owner, or occupant of any dwelling to notify the competent immigration officer in writing using Form TM.30 of any foreign national lodging at that address within 24 hours of their arrival.
non_obvious_actual_reality: This is the landlord's statutory obligation — not the employee's — but failure to file TM.30 directly harms the employee: the Immigration Bureau will reject the employee's 90-day address notifications (Form TM.47) submitted from any address that has no TM.30 on record, rendering the employee non-compliant through no fault of their own. Hotel front desks file TM.30 automatically; private apartment landlords almost universally do not and are oftenunaware of the legal requirement. The fine falls on the landlord, but the practical consequence — a blocked 90-day filing — falls on the employee.
non_obvious_action_required: Before or on the day of arrival, brief the landlord on their TM.30 obligation. Provide a copy of the employee's passport data page and arrival entry stamp. If the landlord refuses, the employee may attend the local Immigration Bureau office to submit TM.30 themselves. Request a stamped receipt and retain it — it is required for 90-day reporting.
source: Immigration Act B.E. 2522 Section 38 — TM.30 Notification of Foreigner Residence

step: Employer submits the employee's work permit application (Form WP.10) to the Department of Employment; employee must attend in person; the physical WP.10 book must be in hand before the employee performs any work
authority: Department of Employment, Ministry of Labour
deadline_label: First business day after arrival — before any work activity whatsoever
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign nationals must obtain a work permit from the Department of Employment before performing any work in Thailand under the Foreign Workers Act B.E. 2551.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The permit is employer-specific and location-specific: it names the employer, type of work, and workplace address. A change of employer, work location, or additional duties for another entity requires an amendment or new permit. The WP.10 must be carried during working hours at all times. Working even one day without a valid WP.10 is a criminal offence punishable by up to five years imprisonment and fines for both employee and employer.
non_obvious_action_required: Arrange for the employer's immigration lawyer or HR representative to accompany the employee to the DOE office on the first business day after arrival. Bring originals and copies of: passport with valid Non-Immigrant B entry stamp, four passport photos (4×6 cm, white background), completed WP.10 form, recent medical certificate, apostilled and translated police clearance, notarised academic credentials in Thai translation, and all WP.3 approval documents. Processing is typically 1–3 business days.
source: Department of Employment — Work Permit for Foreign Nationals (WP.10)

step: If the Non-Immigrant B visa is single-entry, obtain a re-entry permit (Form TM.8) from the Immigration Bureau or airport departure hall before any international travel — departing without it cancels the current permission to stay
deadline_label: Before any international departure; obtain within first week if business travel is anticipated
non_obvious_official_guidance: A foreign national holding a single-entry Non-Immigrant visa who departs Thailand extinguishes their current entry permission. A re-entry permit must be obtained before departure to preserve the validity of the existing stay permission and work permit.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Departing Thailand on a single-entry Non-Immigrant B without a TM.8 voids the entire permission to stay and invalidates the work permit tied to that stay period. The employee would need to re-enter on a fresh Non-Immigrant B obtained abroad and the employer would need to restart the extension of stay process. A multiple re-entry permit costs only a few hundred Thai baht and is purchased in minutes at airport immigration or an Immigration Bureau office — but only before the flight departs, never after.
non_obvious_action_required: Immediately after receiving the WP.10, verify whether the Non-Immigrant B stamp is single-entry or multiple-entry. If single-entry, purchase a multiple re-entry permit (Form TM.8) at the nearest Immigration Bureau office or airport departure hall before the first international journey. Keep the TM.8 stapled adjacent to the visa page.
source: Immigration Bureau Thailand — Re-Entry Permit (Form TM.8)

step: Apply for an annual extension of stay (Form TM.7) at the Immigration Bureau before the initial 90-day entry permission expires; this is a separate in-country step distinct from the Non-Immigrant B visa obtained at the embassy
deadline_label: Apply by day 60–75 of the initial 90-day stay to ensure processing before expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: The Non-Immigrant B visa grants an initial 90-day permission to stay upon entry. To continue working legally beyond those 90 days, the holder must apply for an extension of stay at the Immigration Bureau using Form TM.7, supported by a valid work permit.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Non-Immigrant B visa issued by the embassy abroad is not a 1-year work authorisation — it is only a 90-day entry stamp. The 1-year working stay is a separate extension of stay granted inside Thailand by the Immigration Bureau. Many employees and HR teams discover this two-stage structure only days before the 90-day expiry, creating an overstay risk. The extension is renewable annually and must be renewed together with the work permit.
non_obvious_action_required: At day 60 of the stay (leaving a 30-day processing buffer), submit Form TM.7 at the Immigration Bureau with: passport, WP.10 work permit, company employment confirmation letter, certified DBD registration, the company's most recent Por Por 30 VAT filings, and four passport photographs. The approved extension typically covers 1 year from the original entry date.
source: Immigration Bureau Thailand — Extension of Stay for Non-Immigrant B Visa Holders

step: Register for a Thai taxpayer identification number (TIN) at the Revenue Department district office covering the employee's residential address
deadline_label: Within 60 days of commencement of employment
non_obvious_official_guidance: Individuals deriving assessable income in Thailand must obtain a taxpayer identification number from the Revenue Department to fulfil personal income tax obligations.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many employees assume the employer's payroll system registers them for a TIN automatically or that employer withholding (PND.1) discharges all individual obligations. Neither is true. Without a TIN the employee cannot file an annual return, claim double-tax treaty credits, or receive refunds. Some Revenue District offices allow foreigners to use their passport number informally but a dedicated TIN is the legally correct path.
non_obvious_action_required: Attend the Revenue Department district office for the district of the employee's residence. Bring: passport with valid visa and entry stamp, WP.10 work permit, copy of employment contract, and TM.30 receipt confirming registered residential address. TINs are typically issued the same day at no cost.
source: Revenue Department of Thailand — Personal Income Tax Registration

step: Employer registers the employee with the Social Security Fund (SSF) at the Social Security Office within 30 days of the employee's first working day
authority: Social Security Office, Ministry of Labour
deadline_label: Within 30 days of first working day
source: Social Security Act B.E. 2533 — Section 33 Employee Registration

step: Employer's tax adviser assesses whether the employee will exceed the 180-day threshold for Thai tax residency in the current calendar year, triggering personal income tax liability on worldwide income brought into Thailand
deadline_label: Assess within 30 days of arrival; review again at day 150
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under Section 41 of the Revenue Code, an individual who resides in Thailand for periods aggregating 180 days or more in any tax year is a tax resident and is subject to personal income tax on income derived from sources in Thailand and on foreign-sourced income brought into Thailand in the same tax year in which it was earned.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 'same tax year as earned' condition on foreign income is the critical trap. A tax resident who transfers a home-country bonus or savings earned in the current calendar year into a Thai bank account in the same year owes Thai personal income tax on that amount — even if tax was already withheld abroad. Treaty relief is available under most Thai double-tax treaties but must be actively claimed in the annual filing; it is not applied automatically by the Revenue Department.
non_obvious_action_required: At day 150 of the stay, the employer's tax adviser should recount actual Thailand-presence days. If the 180-day threshold will be crossed: (1) review the applicable double-tax treaty for relief on foreign-sourced income; (2) advise the employee not to transfer current-year foreign income into Thailand without prior advice; (3) begin collating worldwide income documentation for the March 31 annual filing.
source: Revenue Code of Thailand Section 41 — Personal Income Tax Residency

step: File first 90-day address notification (Form TM.47) with the Immigration Bureau; due within 90 days of the arrival entry stamp; the filing window opens 15 days before and closes 7 days after the 90-day mark
deadline_label: Between day 75 and day 97 after arrival (must not miss day 97)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Section 37(5) of the Immigration Act B.E. 2522 requires any foreign national remaining in Thailand for 90 consecutive days to notify the Immigration Bureau of their current address using Form TM.47 within the period commencing 15 days before and ending 7 days after each 90-day interval.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Filing outside the 75–97 day window incurs a THB 2,000 fine per missed report and is recorded on the immigration file, which can complicate extension of stay and visa renewal. Additionally, the TM.30 for the residential address must already be on record at the Immigration Bureau — a missing TM.30 causes TM.47 to be rejected at the counter.
non_obvious_action_required: Set a phone calendar reminder for day 75 after arrival. Confirm TM.30 for the residential address is on record before attending. File online via the Immigration Bureau e-reporting portal, by registered mail, or in person at the local immigration office. Retain the acknowledgement receipt — the date printed on it sets the next 90-day due date.
source: Immigration Act B.E. 2522 Section 37(5) — 90-Day Address Reporting

step: File Form TM.47 with the Immigration Bureau every 90 days; any international departure and re-entry resets the 90-day counter to the new entry date
deadline_label: Every 90 days; window is 15 days before to 7 days after each due date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign nationals must report their address to the Immigration Bureau every 90 days under Section 37(5) of the Immigration Act B.E. 2522.
non_obvious_actual_reality: International travel resets the 90-day counter: upon each re-entry into Thailand a new 90-day period begins from the new entry date, regardless of when the most recent TM.47 was filed. Employees with frequent overseas business trips may find their reporting cycle shifting multiple times per year. A recurring annual calendar reminder will produce systematic errors; the correct approach is to update the next-due date after every passport re-entry stamp.
non_obvious_action_required: After every international journey, note the new entry date in the passport and set a fresh reminder for day 75 after that date. If a trip abroad occurs inside an existing 90-day window the old window is cancelled and the new entry date governs.
source: Immigration Act B.E. 2522 Section 37(5) — 90-Day Address Reporting

step: Employer renews the work permit (WP.10) at the Department of Employment and the employee renews the annual extension of stay (Form TM.7) at the Immigration Bureau — in that sequence — before respective expiry dates each year
authority: Department of Employment (WP.10 renewal); Immigration Bureau (TM.7 renewal)
field_label: Annual Work Permit and Extension of Stay Renewal
deadline_label: Begin preparation 60 days before expiry; submit WP.10 at least 30 days before expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: Work permits must be renewed annually at the Department of Employment. An extension of stay cannot be granted for a period longer than the associated work permit, and a work permit cannot be renewed if the extension of stay has already lapsed.
non_obvious_actual_reality: These are sequential appointments at two separate government offices. The correct order is: (1) renew the work permit at DOE first, receiving the new WP.10; (2) then present the renewed WP.10 to the Immigration Bureau to renew the extension of stay under TM.7. Reversing the order or allowing either to lapse before the other is renewed creates a gap during which the employee is working illegally. Both should be tracked on one shared calendar reminder.
non_obvious_action_required: Begin document preparation 60 days before expiry. WP.10 renewal documents include: current DBD registration, current financial statements, updated Thai and foreign employee headcount (to verify 4:1 ratio), and a company letter confirming the role. After receiving the renewed WP.10, book an Immigration Bureau appointment immediately to renew the extension of stay before it expires.
source: Department of Employment — Annual Work Permit Renewal

step: Employee files annual personal income tax return (Form PND.91 for employment income only, or PND.90 for multiple income types) with the Revenue Department by 31 March of the following year; monthly withholding does not replace the annual filing
field_label: Annual Personal Income Tax Return (PND.91 / PND.90)
deadline_label: 31 March of the following calendar year (online filers receive an extension of approximately 8 days)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Any person deriving assessable income in Thailand must file an annual personal income tax return by 31 March of the following year. Tax residents must additionally declare foreign-sourced income brought into Thailand in the same year as it was earned.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Monthly withholding tax (PND.1) deducted by the employer is an advance payment only — it does not discharge the employee's obligation to file an annual return. Many foreign employees, accustomed to jurisdictions where employer withholding is final, miss the annual filing entirely. Employees who consider themselves non-residents but have Thailand-sourced income — bonuses, benefits, commissions paid by the Thai entity — are still required to file on that income. Treaty relief must be asserted in the return; it is not granted automatically.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a Thai tax adviser to prepare the filing. Gather: Sor.Kor.1 withholding tax certificates from all Thai-entity employers, documentation of any foreign income brought into Thailand during the year, receipts for deductible items (SSF contributions, life insurance premiums, personal allowances). Online filing via the Revenue Department e-Filing portal extends the deadline and is strongly recommended.
source: Revenue Code of Thailand — Personal Income Tax Filing (PND.91 / PND.90)

step: Employer deducts 5% Social Security Fund contribution from the employee's monthly insurable wages (subject to the statutory wage ceiling) and remits both employee and employer shares to the Social Security Office by the 15th of the following month
authority: Social Security Office, Ministry of Labour
source: Social Security Act B.E. 2533 — Section 33 Contribution Obligations

step: Employer withholds personal income tax from the employee's monthly salary applying the progressive rate schedule and remits it to the Revenue Department on Form PND.1 by the 7th of the following month, or the 15th when filing online
field_label: Monthly Withholding Tax on Employment Income (PND.1)
deadline_label: 7th of each following month (15th for online filings)
source: Revenue Code of Thailand — Withholding Tax on Employment Income (PND.1)
